opus-5.5.text:
Sales is one of those functions where a huge share of the work is research, synthesis, and writing, which is exactly what these models are good at. Think about what a good salesperson does before a call: they read up on the company, look at recent news, figure out who the stakeholders are, dig through the CRM to see past interactions, and then draft outreach that's actually tailored. That's hours of knowledge work per account, and most reps simply don't have the time to do it well for every prospect. So they end up sending generic messages, and everyone knows how well those land.

With a model that's connected to your internal data, like your CRM, your product docs, and your past deal history, plus the open web, you can do that prep in seconds and do it for every account, not just the top ten. That changes the math of the job. The rep gets to spend their time on the part that's genuinely human: building the relationship, reading the room, negotiating.

The other reason it's promising is that the value is really legible. In a lot of enterprise AI deployments, it's hard to measure ROI. In sales you've got pipeline, conversion rates, deal velocity. You can run the experiment and see the numbers move. That makes it much easier for a company to get conviction and actually deploy at scale, rather than getting stuck in pilot purgatory.

And finally, the data's already there. Sales orgs have been obsessively logging everything for decades: calls, emails, notes, outcomes. That's a rich foundation for retrieval and for agents that can take real actions, like updating records, scheduling follow-ups, and flagging at-risk deals. So you've got high-value work, a measurable outcome, and the data to ground the model. That combination is pretty rare, and it's why I think sales is one of the first places you'll see AI really transform how a function operates.

r001.rationale: It says a salesperson checks the CRM for past interactions before a call, identifying the company’s interaction history with a prospect as part of pre-meeting research.

r002.rationale: It explains that customer research and tailored preparation help reps do the work well, avoid generic outreach, and prepare for every account, communicating a substantial improvement in salesperson effectiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Sales is interesting because it's one of the few functions in a company where the value of the work is incredibly legible. You know exactly what a closed deal is worth, you know your conversion rates at every stage of the funnel, and you know how much time a rep spends on things that aren't actually selling. So when you introduce a model into that workflow, you can measure the impact almost immediately. That's rare. In a lot of other domains, the ROI of AI is still kind of fuzzy and you're arguing about productivity in the abstract.

The other thing is that so much of sales is language work. It's reading an account, understanding who the stakeholders are, figuring out what they care about, drafting the outreach, following up, summarizing the call, updating the CRM. The actual human part, the relationship and the judgment about when to push and when to back off, is a relatively small slice of the day. Everything around it is research, synthesis, and writing, and that is exactly what these models are good at.

And then there's the data side. Enterprises are sitting on enormous amounts of context about their customers, in emails, call transcripts, support tickets, past deals, and almost none of it gets used because no human has time to read it. A model can. So you can go from a rep working off a name and a title to a rep walking into a conversation with a genuinely informed view of what that customer needs. That's not replacing the salesperson, it's making every rep look like your best rep.

The last reason is more practical. Sales teams are already very comfortable adopting tools. They've been through CRM, through sales engagement platforms, through conversation intelligence. They're used to measuring themselves and trying new things if it moves the number. So the adoption friction is a lot lower than in, say, legal or healthcare, where you have to clear a lot more cultural and regulatory hurdles before anyone will let a model near the work. Put all of that together and it's one of the places where I'd expect the value to show up first and most clearly.

r001.rationale: The response describes using company-held customer context—including emails, call transcripts, support tickets, and past deals—to prepare a rep for a conversation.

r002.rationale: It says the model gives reps a genuinely informed view of customer needs and can make every rep look like the company’s best rep, communicating a substantial improvement in effectiveness.

astra-6.text:
I think sales is interesting because there’s a very clear connection between making someone more productive and creating value for the business. If you can help a salesperson spend less time researching accounts, updating a CRM, or preparing follow-ups, they can spend more time actually talking to customers.

And a lot of that work is language-based. You’re trying to understand what a customer needs, find the relevant information about your product, and communicate why it might be useful to them. Those are tasks where these models can help.

You also have a relatively concrete way to measure whether it’s working. Are people having more productive conversations? Are deals moving faster? Are they closing more business? That makes it easier to justify the investment and learn where the technology is actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response mentions researching accounts and updating a CRM, but does not identify the seller’s company’s interaction history with a prospective customer as research material.

sol-6.1.text:
Sales is interesting because so much of the work is understanding a customer: What do they need? What problem are they trying to solve? And then figuring out whether your product can actually help. That means bringing together information from conversations, emails, your CRM, and your own product documentation. Language models are very good at working with that kind of unstructured information.

You can give a salesperson something that helps them prepare for a meeting, surfaces the right information during a conversation, and takes care of the follow-up afterward. That gives them more time to spend with customers. And there’s a pretty direct way to measure whether it’s useful: Are they spending less time on administrative work? Are they closing more deals? That makes it a compelling place to deploy AI.

r001.rationale: It mentions conversations, emails, and CRM information generally, but does not identify the company’s history of interactions with a prospective customer as material to pre-meeting research.
